newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori leaves Peru for hostage crisis summit.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori leaves Peru for hostage crisis summit.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori left on Friday for a summit in Canada with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to plot an end to the 45-day hostage crisis aware the standoff with Marxist rebels could last months.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo, Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila and several government party legislators, including congressional president Joy Way accompanied Fujimori.

Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canada's ambasssador to Peru, Anthony Vincent -- two members of a commission set to supervise talks between the government and rebels -- also traveled to Canada. The Red Cross -- the final member of the commission -- did not send a representataive to the meeting, scheduled to take place on Saturday in Toronto.

The roughly 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holed up at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima have refused to give up their VIP captives -- including about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats -- unless the government frees 400 jailed comrades.
Fujimori, who refuses to consider the rebels' demand, said on Thursday he was prepared for the six-week-old siege to drag on.

"It could go on a lot longer still. I am patient (to wait) for the hostages to be freed safe and sound ... It could take some weeks, some months," Fujimori said in an interview with Argentina's CVN television network.
The summit with Hashimoto in Toronto was aimed at achieving "a very close coordination," he said. "If we were in an emergency situation we would need to be in close contact."
The two leaders also were expected to discuss recent police maneuvers outside the siege site that have brought criticism from Tokyo.
Hashimoto called several times this week for Fujimori to exercise caution in the deployment of police at the site to prevent "accidents or incidents."

Fujimori admitted to CVN obscene gestures by police that provoked the rebels earlier this week to fire several shots at the officers "were not planned," adding stricter orders to officers were needed.
But he said the moves demonstrated to the MRTA the police were in control of the siege site.
A senior Peruvian government source, speaking on condition of anonymity, insisted Fujimori would not apologize to Hashimoto for the provocative police moves.
Nor would Fujimori use the meeting to seek approval for a military assault on the mined and booby-trapped compound, the source said.

Returning from Canada, the Peruvian president will travel to Washington on Sunday for a meeting on Monday with U.S. President Bill Clinton to thank him for Washington's strong backing during the crisis, government sources said.
Washington did not, however, confirm the meeting and Fujimori said it was not formally scheduled.
Police repeated on Friday their tactics aimed at wearing down the rebels by blasting in the early hours broadcasts of martial music, sirens and the roar of aircraft at the building.
A twin-engine military plane also flew slowly over the site.
Hashimoto said on Thursday the weekend summit would confirm Tokyo and Lima's joint strategy of not "caving in to terrorism."
But he was likely to temper tough talk with a plea that Lima avoid provoking the rebels into harming their hostages, who include two dozen Japanese, officials in Tokyo said.
"The meeting is not meddling with the Peruvian government, but is a discussion," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said his country was chosen to host Saturday's meeting because of its mediating role in the crisis.

The MRTA rebels seized hundreds of guests when they stormed the residence Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception. They released most of the captives but kept those they considered the most important bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, top government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and the Japanese.
